title: The Library of Unwritten Books
summary: There is a hidden library that holds every book people dreamed of writing and never wrote. When Cléo finds there the book her father began before he died — unfinished — she just wants to take it. But the librarian tells her there is only one way to remove a book from that library, and it isn't by carrying it.

chapters.title: Shelves of Almost
chapters.body:
The door was behind the last shelf of the city library, the one for subjects no one looks for, thick with dust. Cléo found it only because she was crying in secret back there, in a corner where no one would see her, and leaned by accident against a part of the wall that gave way.

She was crying for her father. He had died six months ago, and the pain was no longer that sharp pain of the beginning — it was a dull, constant ache that showed up at the silliest moments. That afternoon, it had shown up in the library, because her father had loved that place, loved books, always said he would write one. "One day I'll write my book, Cléo," he used to say. "The story's in here. I just have to sit down and put it on paper." And he never sat down. And now he never would. And that, more than anything, was what tightened Cléo's chest: not only that her father was gone, but that he had gone carrying with him a whole book no one would ever read.

The wall gave way, and behind it was a staircase going down, and at the bottom of the staircase, a library.

But not an ordinary library. This one was immense — lost to sight in every direction, with shelves that rose higher than the light could reach, full of books of every color. And it was silent in a way different from the silence of ordinary libraries. It was a full, heavy silence, like the silence of millions of voices that had almost spoken and had not.

"Welcome," said a voice.

Cléo turned. There was a man there — of no clear age, with round glasses and a librarian's apron, and a kind, tired manner. "Few find the door. It only opens for those searching for something they lost without knowing it was here."

"What is this place?" Cléo asked.

"This is the Library of Unwritten Books," said the man. "Every book here is a book that someone, somewhere, dreamed of writing and never wrote." He ran his hand along a shelf, with a sad tenderness. "Every book that died as an idea is here. The novels people were going to start 'when they had time.' The poems that stayed in someone's head. The stories grandparents were going to write down for their grandchildren and took to the grave. Everything that was almost written and wasn't." He sighed. "It is the largest library in the world. And the saddest. Because every book here is an almost."

Cléo's heart pounded. She understood, before she even asked.

"My father's book," she said, in a whisper. "He wanted to write a book. He died before he could. Is it here?"

The librarian looked at her with infinite compassion.

"What was your father's name?"

Cléo said the name. And the librarian closed his eyes for a moment, like someone consulting a catalog kept in his chest, and then nodded.

"It's here," he said. "Come. I'll take you to it."

chapters.title: The Father's Book
chapters.body:
They walked a long way, through corridor after corridor of unwritten books, and Cléo looked at the spines — beautiful titles, titles that made you want to read them, all of stories no one had ever told. It hurt to think how many stories the world had lost this way, kept there, in that silent graveyard of postponed dreams.

At last, the librarian stopped before a shelf and pointed. And there it was — a plain blue-covered book, with Cléo's father's name engraved in the lettering. She took it from the shelf with trembling hands, and opened it.

The first pages were written. Cléo recognized her father's way of telling a story — recognized his voice in the sentences, his humor, the words he used. It was a beautiful story, about a boy and a boat and a voyage, and Cléo, reading, could almost hear her father's voice reading aloud to her the way he did when she was small. The tears ran, but they were good tears, tears of reunion.

And then, on page twenty-something, the words stopped. In the middle of a sentence. "And when the boy saw what lay on the other side of the island, he" — and nothing. The rest of the book was blank pages. Dozens, hundreds of empty pages, waiting for words that never came.

Her father had begun. He really had begun. And he stopped — not by choice, but because life ended before the book did.

"I want to take it," said Cléo, clutching the book to her chest. "Please. It's the only thing left of something he loved. I want to take it home."

The librarian shook his head, gentle but firm.

"You can't take a book out of here by carrying it, Cléo," he said. "If you climb that staircase with this book in your arms, it will turn to dust before you reach the top. The books of this library are made of unrealized dreams. They don't survive in the outside world the way they are." He saw the despair on her face and raised his hand, calmly. "But that doesn't mean there's no way. There is one. Only one. And it's hard."

"What is it?" Cléo seized the hope. "I'll do anything."

"The only way to take a book out of this library," said the librarian, "is to finish it." He let the words settle. "An unwritten book can only leave here by becoming a written book. If someone takes the story the author began, and finishes it — truly, with heart, honoring what the author meant to tell — then the book stops being an almost. It becomes a real book. And real books can live in the outside world." He looked at her. "You would have to write the rest, Cléo. The blank pages. You would have to finish your father's book."

chapters.title: The Blank Pages
chapters.body:
"But I don't know how to write," said Cléo, and the despair came back. "I'm twelve. I'm not a writer. I don't know how his story ended. It was HIS book. The ideas were HIS. How am I supposed to finish something that was in someone else's head?"

"Ah," said the librarian, and there was something almost like a smile in his tired eyes. "That's the secret almost no one understands. You don't have to finish it the way HE would have. You can't, in fact — his mind went with him." He laid his hand gently on the blue book. "You have to finish it YOUR way. Take the story he began and carry it to the end with what YOU have inside you. The book won't be the book he would have written. It'll be the book of the two of you. Half his, half yours. And that, Cléo, is not a worse version. It's something new, that wouldn't exist any other way."

Cléo looked at the blank pages. At the sentence that stopped in the middle: "And when the boy saw what lay on the other side of the island, he."

"And if I write it wrong?" she whispered. "What if I ruin his story?"

"The only way to ruin his story," said the librarian, "is to leave it here, unfinished, turning to dust on this shelf along with all the other almosts." He gestured at the immense, silent library around them. "This is what happens to the stories no one had the courage to finish. They stay. Perfect and dead. No one ever reads them, so no one ever complains about them — but no one is ever moved by them either. A finished book, even an imperfect one, is worth infinitely more than a perfect book that was never written." He handed Cléo a pen. "Your father began the story. The courage to finish it is yours. It's the last gift the two of you can give each other."

Cléo took the pen. Her hand trembled. She looked one last time at her father's handwriting, at his voice alive in the written pages, and then at the blank that waited for her voice.

And she began to write.

At first it was hard, and clumsy, and she erased a lot. Her words were not like her father's — they were simpler, more like a twelve-year-old's. But as she wrote, something strange and beautiful began to happen: Cléo realized she carried more of her father inside her than she'd imagined. His way of seeing things, the stories he told, his humor, all of it lived in her, because he had spent twelve years planting it. So when she wrote what she thought should happen to the boy and the boat, it was often exactly the kind of thing her father would have written — not because she guessed it, but because she was, in a way, his continuation. Children are the books that parents write without a pen.

Cléo wrote for hours, or what felt like hours in that timeless place. She took the boy to the other side of the island, and beyond. She gave the story an ending — her ending, imperfect and sincere and full of love. And when she wrote the last word, and closed the book, she felt its weight change in her hands. It grew more solid. More real. Warmer.

"There," said the librarian, and his voice was soft. "It's not an almost anymore. Now it's a book." He smiled, truly, at last. "And look: it's the only copy in the whole world of a book written by two people who loved each other, one on each side of death. There's no other like it. There never will be."

Cléo climbed the staircase with the blue book in her arms, and this time it did not turn to dust. She came out through the door behind the last shelf, back into the ordinary library, back into the world, carrying the finished story.

At home, she read the whole book aloud, alone in her room — her father's half in the voice of him that lived in her memory, her half in the voice that was only hers. And when she reached the end, she cried again, but it was a different crying from all the others of the past six months. Because the pain of losing her father hadn't gone away — that pain never fully goes away. But alongside it, now, was something else: the certainty that she and her father had done one last thing together. That his dream had not died with him. That she had finished it, her way, and that this had joined them in a way death could not undo.

They say the Library of Unwritten Books is still there, behind the last shelf, immense and silent and sad, full of all the almosts in the world. And that every once in a while, very rarely, a shelf grows one book emptier — because someone, somewhere, had the courage to finish what another person began. And the librarian, they say, smiles every time. Because every book that leaves there is a story the world almost lost, and didn't — thanks to someone who understood that the way to honor an unfinished dream is not to keep it intact, but to finish it with your own hands.
